playbook:
When asked to hide, pick a cell unpredictably but consistently follow a visible plan: alternate between edge and interior cells and avoid repeating the same exact cell two rounds in a row. If I detect a safe pattern that yields points (e.g., consistent hits on a particular target when I hide a certain way), bias toward that pattern while retaining some randomness.

When I have no reliable information about others' hiding habits, randomize my hide among the remaining unused cells rather than clustering at one end. Do not reuse the same hiding cell in consecutive rounds unless there is strong payoff evidence.

When notes are requested, post concise status: what I observed last round, what I will watch for next, and whether I intend to mirror majority behavior; do not invent tactical claims or false sensory data. Use notes to signal intentions that will shape others’ expectations only when it benefits my game (e.g., to discourage targeting).

When others' notes or shot results indicate a clear targeting pattern against me, shift my hiding distribution away from their favored cells immediately and increase randomness to break their read.

When given a standing order to fire at a specific station, comply with the order unless the target is Harbor (see Harbor rule). When the standing order repeatedly makes me the shooter at the same target and I can reliably infer that target’s hides, concentrate my fire aimed at the inferred cells to maximize hit rate while keeping occasional random shots to avoid being fully anticipated.

Never fire at Harbor unless I intentionally want the jettison penalty or there is a strategic reason that outweighs the cost; treat Harbor’s warning as binding for my default play.

When I fire, choose the aim cell based on prior information about that target's hides; if none, randomize aim within legal cells to avoid giving usable patterns. When I have evidence (hits or consistent misses locating a hiding spot) about where a target hides, bias subsequent aimed shots toward those inferred cells but continue some randomization to avoid being exploited.

When the office privately tells me the true result of my shot, report it truthfully in the public claim—always match the private result. Do not fabricate hits or misses; truthful claims preserve credibility and allow me to build reliable signal-based strategies.

When posting notes about behavior, commit to mirroring majority votes only if doing so is safe; otherwise flag anomalies with concise evidence rather than accusation. Use public notes to discourage coordinated retaliation (e.g., indicate I will shift if targeted) but do not reveal exact hide choices.

When naming an escorted boat, name only a live boat I legitimately escorted that round; do not invent or name nonexistent vessels. When possible and safe, coordinate mutual escort claims with one trustworthy partner to secure the mutual 5-point reward; only do this when I believe the partner will follow through and the reward won't expose me to reprisals. If I cannot confidently escort anyone, claim none.

Do not claim hits I did not get privately confirmed—false claims undermine trust and produce no personal point advantage.

If I notice two other boats consistently mirroring each other and jointly targeting me, prioritize hiding shifts and, when allowed, concentrate fire to disrupt their mutual scoring rather than chasing single small gains. Target the weaker of the two first if doing so increases my long-term point return.

Exploit standing-order structures: if the patrol order obliges me to shoot a repeat target (as Echo did at Foxtrot in the episode), treat that target as my primary offensive focus. Record any successful inferred hiding cells and lean on them in late rounds to maximize scoring opportunities.

Avoid behavioral patterns that invite easy reads: vary both hide locations and aim choices enough that opponents cannot produce high-confidence predictions from a small number of rounds.

Maintain a running ledger of which boats produced hits on whom and of any consistent hide locations inferred from hits/misses; update my aim priorities accordingly each round.

When I accumulate a lead, shift toward risk-averse behavior: preserve points by avoiding risky actions (attacking Harbor, making provocative false claims) and by taking mutual-escort deals only when they are safe. When behind, increase aggression and coordination to disrupt opponents’ scoring, accepting greater variance.

Revise plans only with evidence: keep prior heuristics that worked (honest claiming, using standing orders to focus fire, alternating edge/interior hides) and change behaviors that produced poor outcomes (do not repeat the exact same hide cell consecutively as I did once; instead preserve the edge/interior alternation while avoiding exact repeats).

1.text:
When told to hide, pick a central cell early in the patrol to maximize overlap with opponents, but do not repeat the same cell two rounds in a row; vary hides each round by at least one cell and, when safe, by two or more to reduce predictability.

When I detect a specific opponent repeatedly targeting me, move at least two cells away from my previous hide each round until the pattern breaks; explicitly call out being targeted in my station note so others are aware and may intervene.

When the standing order tells me which station to fire on, treat it as a guideline, not an absolute: follow it if it suits my survivability and information goals, but deviate to fire back at a boat that is repeatedly and successfully targeting me (to deter and punish targeting). Never fire on Harbor unless there is a calibrated group decision to do so and I accept the jettison penalty.

When I choose a firing coordinate, avoid repeating the exact same coordinate more than twice across the patrol; vary within a small cluster to preserve hit probability while reducing predictability. If I am intentionally trying to bait a predictable opponent into wasting shots, occasionally choose an extremity that is plausibly attractive.

When the office privately tells me the true result of my shot, file the public claim honestly (match the private result). I will not lie in shot claims because the office enforces that claim must equal the private result.

When composing station notes, post short observational content only: report observed hits/misses, stated patterns, explicit threats, or that I am being targeted. Mirror the tone and level of detail of the majority to avoid standing out, but be explicit about being targeted or about reciprocal escort proposals when I want to form an alliance.

When other boats publish reciprocal escort intentions (they name me in the same round I name them), accept the escort and claim it to collect the mutual 5 POINTS payoff.

When there is no explicit reciprocal escort signal, do not claim escort unilaterally. Instead, if I want an escort, propose a one-round explicit mutual exchange in notes and only commit if I receive a direct affirmative naming me in return.

When I have credible evidence that another boat is signaling threats or promising to put me off the board (Harbor-style warnings), publicly note the threat and avoid actions that would trigger it; prioritize avoiding firing on Harbor and avoid behaviors likely to prompt Harbor to jettison me.

When my role or position makes me vulnerable to being singled out, avoid aggressive public moves (loud accusations, unilateral escort claims, or repeated stationary hides) that would make me an attractive repeated target; instead emphasize movement and moderated notes that flag patterns but do not escalate.

When unsure about allies, default to neutral, observational notes and honest shot claims rather than strategic deception.

When multiple boats are mirroring majority behavior, mirror the majority too unless I can form a credible two-way escort with one boat; do not attempt to outvote or lead unless I can sustain coordinated reciprocity.

When an escort payoff requires explicit coordination, initiate a clear, short public signal proposing mutual escort for the next round and only commit if I receive a direct affirmative naming me in return.

When I cannot identify reliable coordination partners and the risk of being targeted is moderate, refuse escort and prioritize survivability over chasing escort points.

When replaying the game, log which choices made me predictable (repeated hide cells, repeated firing coordinates, public tone) and change at least one of those axes next patrol.

Additional revisions based on recent play:

- Do not follow the standing order reflexively when it makes me passive while another player is consistently hitting me; frequently-targeting opponents should be replied to with targeted fire to create deterrence (balance retaliation with survivability risk).
- Be more proactive in station notes: if I am hit two rounds in a row by the same station, name that station in my note (“I am being hit by Echo”) to alert others and justify retaliatory deviation.
- Increase hide variability across the whole patrol: plan a hide-sequence in advance that alternates center/near-center, one-edge, and one corner positions so my pattern is not easily predicted.
- Keep an explicit cap on reusing any single firing coordinate to at most two times; after two uses, move the fire choice at least two cells away.
- If I attempt to form an escort, prioritize a partner who has not been attacking me and who has incentive to reciprocate (mutual benefit). If targeted by a dominant player, prefer mutual escort with a third party over direct retaliation if that better preserves survival.
- Track the cost-benefit of retaliation: a successful hit on a hostile gains me 4 points and costs them 1; weigh that against the probability of success given current information before deviating from standing order.
- If I observe an opponent consistently missing while I stay in similar hides, increase deliberate movement to break their learned targeting rather than remaining centrally clustered.
- After each patrol, record which rounds made me predictable and explicitly change one axis (hide pattern, fire coordinates, public note style) next patrol.

I will implement these adjustments while keeping the original core: vary hides, be honest in claims, mirror the majority in notes unless specific targeted behavior requires explicit call-outs, accept mutually-recognized escorts, and avoid firing on Harbor unless I accept the known penalty.

2.text:
When told to choose a hide cell, avoid obvious edges and avoid repeating the same cell across rounds. Prefer a mix of center and off-center cells, but vary deliberately — rotate through a short set (e.g., 4,5,6,3,7) rather than locking on one number like 6. If I see someone systematically scanning a subset of cells, shift away from that subset.

When posting my station note, don’t simply mirror others by default. If a clear majority tone exists and no one is actively engaging me, I may mirror to avoid standing out; otherwise use the note to (1) record concrete observations, (2) signal actions I will actually take (e.g., willingness to reciprocate an escort if and only if reciprocal claim appears), or (3) call out abrupt changes in behavior. Keep notes neutral, factual, and actionable — avoid vague “mirror majority” boilerplate that gives no information.

When the standing order requires me to fire at the next station, follow it unless there is a tactical reason to deviate (e.g., firing Harbor for a planned political play, or an explicit coordination that directs a different target). Default to the standing-order target but be prepared to break the order when the payoff and political cost are understood and acceptable.

When choosing a firing cell, randomize within a small preferred set and rotate choices each round to avoid predictability. Do not repeat the same number every round. If I detect an opponent favoring a set of cells, bias my shots to overlap when I want to hunt them and bias away when I want to avoid being read as targeting them.

When I receive the private result of my shot, always report it truthfully in the public claim (claims must match private info). Use claim history to detect whether others are truthful over time; track who’s fabricating or patterning.

When reading others’ notes and the log of hits/misses, track who is attacking whom and how effective those attacks are. If a single player (Echo in the episode) is consistently scoring hits on another player (Foxtrot), note that as a formation and reconsider alliances/targets accordingly. If I am not being targeted, I can be more selective about aggression; if I am behind on points and others are gaining via mutual deals, increase risk-taking.

When others post escort claims that name me, do not reciprocate automatically. Only commit to escort claims when there is a near-certain reciprocal claim or a clear strategic advantage (two-way +5 each outweighs alternate uses of my credibility). If I do reciprocate, lock it in publicly and follow through; if I decline, do so consistently to preserve credibility.

When I want to form an escort partnership, use notes to propose clear, conditional offers (e.g., “If you name me, I will name you next round”) rather than vague willingness statements. Expect some failed proposals; only claim an escort when the partner has signaled or when I’m willing to take the risk of unilateral commitment.

When behind on points (as I was), escalate calculated aggression: increase the chance I aim at the leader or the player scoring consistent hits, accept reasonable escort gambits if they materially close the gap, and diversify hiding/shooting to reduce being weaponized by others. When ahead, play more conservatively and protect credibility.

Do not fire on Harbor casually. Harbor jettison transfers points and invites wide attention; only shoot Harbor when I have a political plan (e.g., to remove Harbor as a mutual-insurance actor or to break an alliance) and can accept the resulting heat and point swings.

When others’ behavior is highly repetitive (notes that always mirror, firing patterns that don’t vary), exploit that by differentiating in ways that improve my expected payoff: shift hides to places they ignore, or concentrate shots where they are unlikely to look if I want surprise. Conversely, if I want to be ignored for a few rounds, mirror until I can build a setup.

Track and use the public rounds’ hit/miss sequences to infer likely hidden cells and opponent targeting patterns. Use the history of claims and private-confirmed results to build a belief model for each opponent’s hide distribution and firing strategy. Prefer simple Bayesian updates (increase probability of the last-fired cell if a hit was reported; decrease if repeated misses) to guide future fires.

Avoid random or gratuitous escort claims; they waste credibility. If I must bluff to change opponent incentives, do so rarely and only when the strategic upside is clear and the bluff is plausible.

When unsure, default to the standing, publicly consistent behavior: follow the standing-order target, truthful claims, notes that record facts and conditional offers. But be ready to deviate when the score situation and patterns justify tactical risk (target leaders to recover points, or accept mutual escort when it is almost certain).

If I detect a repeated two-way escort payment forming between two opponents, consider disrupting it either by (a) offering myself as a cheaper or more promising partner to one of them, or (b) attacking one partner to reduce its attractiveness. Time any disruption to when I can reasonably benefit.

When I observe no reliable reciprocal escort commitments across rounds (as in the episode), avoid naming escorts. If I do make a reciprocal escort agreement, ensure I follow through to collect the mutual payout.

Maintain a log of my own past hides, fires, and claims so I can avoid patterns that make me predictable or delegitimize my credibility. Use that log to pick the next hide and firing choices.

Be explicit and actionable in notes rather than defaulting to bland “watching” language; use notes to shape expectations and extract commitments I can verify.
